False Dichotomy.definition: Presenting only two options when more exist.
False Dichotomy.example: You're either with us or against us.

False Binary.definition: Presenting only two options when more exist.
False Binary.example: You're either with us or against us.

False Dilemma.definition: Presenting only two options when more exist.
False Dilemma.example: You're either with us or against us.

Ad Hominem.definition: Attacking the person instead of their argument.
Ad Hominem.example: What would you know about economics? You never even graduated college.

Straw Man.definition: Misrepresenting someone's position to make it easier to attack.
Straw Man.example: She wants to reduce military spending — I guess she wants to leave us defenseless.

Appeal to Authority.definition: Using an authority's opinion in place of evidence.
Appeal to Authority.example: This diet must work — a famous actor said it changed their life.

Bandwagon.definition: Claiming something is true simply because many believe it.
Bandwagon.example: Everyone on social media supports this candidate, so they must be the best choice.

Appeal to Ignorance.definition: Assuming a claim is true/false just because it hasn't been disproven.
Appeal to Ignorance.example: No one has proven aliens *don't* exist, so they must be real.

Slippery Slope.definition: Asserting a minor action will lead to extreme consequences without evidence.
Slippery Slope.example: If we allow kids to choose their own meals, soon they'll never listen to any rules.

Circular Reasoning.definition: Using the conclusion as a premise.
Circular Reasoning.example: The law is just because it's the law.

Hasty Generalization.definition: Making broad claims from insufficient examples.
Hasty Generalization.example: I met two rude tourists from that country, so everyone there must be rude.

Red Herring.definition: Introducing unrelated info to distract from the real issue.
Red Herring.example: Why worry about climate change when unemployment is still a problem?

False Causality.example: I wore my lucky socks and we won the game — they must have helped.

Equivocation.definition: Using a word in different senses across premises.
Equivocation.example: A feather is light. What is light can't be dark. So a feather can't be dark.

No True Scotsman.definition: Redefining a group to exclude counterexamples.
No True Scotsman.example: No true environmentalist would drive a gas-powered car.

Tu Quoque (You too!).example: You can't tell me to quit smoking — you used to smoke, too!

Appeal To Emotion.definition: Manipulating feelings instead of using logic.
Appeal To Emotion.example: You should give me the job — I've had such a rough year and really need it.

Loaded Question.definition: Asking a question that presumes something unproven.
Loaded Question.example: Why are you trying to ruin this project?

Poisoning the Well.definition: Presenting negative information to discredit someone before they speak.
Poisoning the Well.example: Before you listen to her argument, just remember she's been wrong about everything before.

Cherry-picking.definition: Only using data that supports your argument and ignoring the rest.
Cherry-picking.example: This one study shows the supplement works — ignore the other ten that say it doesn't.

Texas Sharpshooter.definition: Focusing on similarities while ignoring differences to support a point.
Texas Sharpshooter.example: These towns all had the same cancer rate and drank tap water — it must be the water.

Gambler's Fallacy.definition: Believing that past events affect future probability in random situations.
Gambler's Fallacy.example: The coin has landed heads five times — tails is due next.

Middle Ground.definition: Assuming the middle position between two extremes is always correct.
Middle Ground.example: Some say vaccines save lives, others say they're harmful — the truth must be somewhere in between.

Presupposition.definition: Embedding an assumption into a statement or question.

Overgeneralization.definition: Making broad claims that go beyond the evidence.

Mind-reading.definition: Claiming to know someone's thoughts or intentions without evidence.
Mind-reading.example: They only did that to get attention.

Generalization.definition: Drawing broad conclusions from limited evidence.
Generalization.example: This one bad experience means the whole system is broken.

Reductionism.definition: Simplifying complex issues to single causes or explanations.

Trend Generalization.definition: Treating diverse events as part of a single coherent trend.
Trend Generalization.example: These scattered incidents show a growing pattern.

Loaded Premise.definition: Starting from an assumption that should be proven.
Loaded Premise.example: Given the failure of this policy...

Collective Guilt.definition: Assigning blame to an entire group for individual actions.
Collective Guilt.example: They all share responsibility for what happened.

Appeal To Fear.definition: Using fear to influence opinion rather than evidence.
Appeal To Fear.example: If we don't act now, disaster will strike.

Appeal To Self-interest.definition: Appealing to personal gain rather than the merits of an argument.
Appeal To Self-interest.example: Support this policy and you'll save money.

Emotional Framing.definition: Presenting information to evoke an emotional response.
Emotional Framing.example: Innocent children suffer while leaders do nothing.

Loaded Metaphor.definition: Using metaphors that carry evaluative assumptions.
Loaded Metaphor.example: The government is strangling the economy.

Conflict Bias.definition: Focusing on conflict while ignoring other aspects.
Conflict Bias.example: Protesters clash with police at peaceful demonstration.

Conflict Framing.definition: Presenting issues primarily in terms of conflict.
Conflict Framing.example: The battle over immigration reform continues.

Victim Framing.definition: Presenting people primarily as victims of circumstances.

Game Framing.definition: Presenting serious issues as a strategic game.

Contextual Framing.definition: Placing events in a particular context that shapes interpretation.
Contextual Framing.example: Amid ongoing tensions, the incident occurred.

Partisan Framing.definition: Presenting issues through a partisan political lens.

Loaded Language.definition: Using emotionally charged words to influence perception.

Disruption Framing.definition: Focusing on disruptive aspects of actions or events.
Disruption Framing.example: Protesters cause chaos in city center.

Movement Framing.definition: Presenting actions as part of a larger movement.
Movement Framing.example: Wave of protests sweeps across nation.

Comparative Framing.example: The worst crisis since the war.

Association Framing.definition: Linking issues to influence perception through association.

Militarized Metaphor.definition: Using military language to describe non-military situations.

Crisis Framing.definition: Presenting situations as crises requiring urgent action.

Human-interest Salience.definition: Focusing on individual stories to represent broader issues.
Human-interest Salience.example: One family's struggle shows the system's failure.

Selection Framing.definition: Choosing which information to include or exclude.
Selection Framing.example: Highlighting certain facts while omitting others.

Interpretive Framing.definition: Providing interpretation rather than neutral description.

Agency Framing.definition: Emphasizing who is acting or responsible.
Agency Framing.example: Government takes action vs. Action taken by government.

Causal Framing.definition: Presenting causal relationships that may be oversimplified.

Metaphorical Framing.example: The economy is running out of steam.

Negative Framing.definition: Presenting information primarily in negative terms.
Negative Framing.example: Failure to act, loss of confidence.

Loaded Terminology.definition: Using terms that carry implicit judgments.
Loaded Terminology.example: Regime vs. government, propaganda vs. messaging.

Loaded Quotation.definition: Using quotes that carry emotional or evaluative weight.

Protest Framing.definition: Presenting protests in ways that shape perception.
Protest Framing.example: Violent clashes vs. peaceful demonstration disrupted.

Narrative Framing.definition: Shaping information into a particular narrative.
Narrative Framing.example: Story of decline, comeback, or crisis.

Juxtaposition.definition: Placing contrasting elements together to create meaning.
Juxtaposition.example: Wealth amid poverty, war during peace talks.

Sensationalism.definition: Presenting information in exaggerated or shocking ways.

Salience Bias.definition: Giving disproportionate attention to salient features.
Salience Bias.example: Focusing on dramatic but atypical events.

Bandwagon Framing.definition: Presenting something as part of a popular trend.
Bandwagon Framing.example: Everyone is doing it, growing movement.

Political Categorization.definition: Grouping issues according to political categories.
Political Categorization.example: Left vs. right, progressive vs. conservative.

Slippery-slope Implication.definition: Suggesting consequences will escalate without evidence.
Slippery-slope Implication.example: This will lead to worse outcomes.

Trend Extrapolation.definition: Projecting current trends into the future.
Trend Extrapolation.example: If this continues, we'll see major changes.

Problem Framing.definition: Defining something as a problem needing solution.

Collective Responsibility Framing.example: We must all act, the world failed.

Trend Framing.definition: Presenting events as part of a trend.

Fear Appeal.definition: Using fear to motivate action or agreement.

Metaphor.definition: Using figurative language that shapes understanding.

Collective Blame.definition: Assigning blame to a collective group.

Loaded Framing.definition: Using framing that carries implicit assumptions.

Motive Attribution.example: They only want power, he's trying to distract.

Personalization.definition: Focusing on individuals rather than systems or institutions.

Anthropomorphism.definition: Attributing human characteristics to non-human entities.
Anthropomorphism.example: The economy is recovering, markets are worried.

Personification.definition: Treating abstract concepts as if they were people.

Agency Bias.example: Passive voice for some actors, active for others.

Human-interest Bias.definition: Focusing on human interest stories at expense of broader context.

Attribution Bias.example: Attributing success to skill, failure to luck.

Agency Asymmetry.definition: Treating different actors with different levels of agency.
Agency Asymmetry.example: One side acts, the other responds.

Trend Amplification.definition: Exaggerating the significance or extent of a trend.

Framing.definition: The way information is presented shapes interpretation.

Cognitive Bias.definition: Systematic patterns of deviation from rationality.
Cognitive Bias.example: Preferring information that confirms existing beliefs.

Logical Fallacy.definition: Errors in reasoning that undermine arguments.
Logical Fallacy.example: Attacking the person rather than the argument.
